name: Must Enable New Innovations
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Third Test: Does It Open New Doors?
lesson.summary: This section explains the final GPT criterion ,  that a true general-purpose technology must make entirely new products, services, or business models possible ,  and shows why quantum computing cannot yet be judged against it.
lesson.body:
You already know that a general-purpose technology has to be pervasive and to keep improving over time. The third test asks something different: does the technology open doors that were simply locked before it existed? A GPT isn't just a faster way to do old things ,  it becomes a platform that other people build on top of, creating goods and services that had no equivalent in the pre-GPT world.

Electricity is the clearest historical illustration. Early on, factories just swapped their steam engines for electric motors and kept the same layout, because machinery had always been arranged around one central power source. The real transformation came later, when factories realized electric power could be distributed to individual machines wherever they were needed. That single change in wiring logic didn't just make production a bit faster ,  it made possible entirely new factory layouts, new production methods, and eventually new consumer goods that ran on household current. The technology became a foundation other innovations were built on, not just an upgrade to existing ones.

This is the bar quantum computing has to clear, and right now it hasn't. Every publicly demonstrated quantum computation to date is either a proof-of-concept run on a small, noisy machine or a task that, while impressive as an engineering feat, doesn't correspond to a product or business model that couldn't exist without it. Nobody is running a company today whose core service depends on a quantum computer doing something no classical computer could do. Contrast this with the internet, which almost immediately enabled things like real-time global communication platforms and online marketplaces that simply had no classical analog ,  you could point to the new thing and say "this exists because of that technology." Quantum computing hasn't produced that pointing exercise yet.

Part of the reason is structural, not just a matter of waiting a bit longer. The applications people talk about ,  breaking certain forms of encryption, simulating complex molecules accurately enough to design new drugs or materials, solving optimization problems at a scale classical computers can't touch ,  all depend on fault-tolerant quantum computers, meaning machines that can run long, deep computations while automatically correcting the errors that noise introduces along the way. That hardware doesn't exist yet. So the honest state of things is: the innovations that would satisfy this criterion are hypothetical, resting on hardware that is itself still hypothetical at the scale required.

This creates a genuine problem for anyone trying to evaluate quantum computing as an investment today. You can't test whether a platform enables new innovations until the platform is mature enough to be built on, but investment decisions are being made now, based on the assumption that it eventually will. That's not necessarily wrong ,  early electricity investors couldn't have proven the factory-layout revolution either ,  but it means the third GPT test currently sits unanswered rather than passed. Recognizing that gap, and not quietly filling it in with optimism, is the skeptical move this book keeps asking you to make.
